Air from that high flows outward, and toward Southern California it must descend from elevations of 1–1.5 km down through the mountain passes and canyons to the coast.

Descending air warms by compression at the dry adiabatic rate, about 9.8 °C per kilometre, and since the source air was desert-dry to begin with, its relative humidity crashes — often below 10–15%. The passes funnel and accelerate the flow, so gusts of 40–60 mph are common in favoured canyons. Autumn is the season because that's when the interior high is strong while the coastal ocean is still warm, maximising the pressure contrast. The fire danger is the compound effect: vegetation already cured by the long dry summer, humidity in single digits, and winds that carry embers miles ahead of a fire front. When forecasters say 'Santa Ana conditions', firefighters hear the whole sentence.
What's the difference between the fog we get on calm autumn mornings and San Francisco's summer fog?

Same white nothing, opposite machinery. Your autumn fog is radiation fog: on a long, clear, calm night the ground radiates heat to space and cools, chilling the air touching it to its dew point. Water vapour condenses into a shallow layer, thickest in low ground where cold air pools. It forms from the ground up, peaks around dawn, and 'burns off' as the sun warms the surface — really it evaporates from below once the ground warms.

San Francisco's is advection fog: warm, moist Pacific air is carried over the cold California Current (kept cold by coastal upwelling), chilling the air from below to saturation while it moves. It can arrive at any hour, pour through the Golden Gate like a fluid, persist for days under an inversion, and it peaks in summer — 'June Gloom' season — precisely because the land-sea temperature contrast is greatest then. One fog is made by the ground cooling the air; the other by cold water cooling moving air. Your forecast question is 'will tonight be clear and calm?'; theirs is 'which way is the wind blowing?'
Why does lake-effect snow peak in late fall and fade by February even though it's colder then?

Because lake effect runs on contrast, not cold alone. The engine needs the lake surface much warmer than the air crossing it — a difference of roughly 13 °C or more between the water and the air at 850 mb. In November and December the lakes still hold summer's heat (water cools slowly) while arctic outbreaks already arrive at full strength, so the contrast is maximal and the lakes are ice-free, evaporating freely.

By February two things have changed. The lakes themselves have cooled, shrinking the temperature difference. And ice cover spreads — a frozen lake is capped: evaporation nearly stops, and the surface the wind crosses is now snow-covered ice at air temperature rather than open water. The machine doesn't slow because the air got too cold; it slows because its fuel supply froze over. Shallow Lake Erie usually freezes first and its snowbelts quiet earliest; deep Lake Superior may keep some open water, and some lake effect, all winter.
On calm nights our valley floor is 10 degrees colder than the hillsides halfway up. Why does cold air pool downhill?

Because cold air is dense air, and on calm nights it behaves like a slow liquid. After sunset the ground radiates heat away; the air in contact with sloping ground cools, becomes heavier than the air beside it at the same altitude, and slides downhill — a katabatic drainage flow, usually just a gentle creep. It collects in valley bottoms and frost hollows, deepening through the night.

The hillside halfway up sits above the pool: it's in the 'thermal belt', where temperatures stay several degrees warmer — which is why orchards and vineyards are planted on slopes rather than valley floors, and why citrus growers obsess over cold-air drainage. The same physics at continental scale drives the fierce katabatic winds off Antarctica and Greenland, where an entire ice sheet's worth of chilled air pours toward the coast. For your forecast, the practical read: on clear, calm nights, valley-bottom temperatures will undershoot the official forecast (which is often measured at an airport on flat ground), and the first and last frosts of the season always arrive in the hollows first.
Why is the city always warmer than the suburbs at night, sometimes by 5 degrees or more?

That's the urban heat island, and nighttime is when it peaks. Cities are built of asphalt, concrete, and masonry — materials that absorb solar energy all day and release it slowly all night — while suburbs and countryside are vegetated, and plants cool themselves and the air by evaporating water. Add waste heat from vehicles, industry, and air conditioners (which pump indoor heat outdoors), plus street canyons that trap outgoing radiation between building faces, and the urban core simply cannot cool at the rural rate.

During the day the difference is modest, because sunshine dominates both. After sunset the countryside cools fast under clear skies while the city leaks stored heat — so the gap maxes out in the early morning hours, often 3–6 °C in large cities, more in calm, clear conditions. It matters beyond comfort: heat islands worsen heat-wave nights (the dangerous part of a heat wave is the night that never cools), shift frost dates, and can even steer thunderstorm outflows. Airport thermometers, often sited at the urban edge, have watched this effect grow with the city around them.
What is the 'marine layer' that gives California its grey May and June mornings?

It's a shallow blanket of cool, moist ocean air that forms over the cold California Current and slides onshore under an inversion. The setup: the Pacific High strengthens in late spring, its subsiding air warms aloft, while the ocean below stays cold from upwelling. Air travelling over that cold water is chilled to saturation, forming low stratus cloud — a cloud deck often only a few hundred metres thick, capped by the warm inversion like a lid.

At night and in the morning, the layer deepens and pushes inland through gaps in the coastal hills; by afternoon, inland heating erodes it from below and it retreats to the coast — 'morning low clouds, afternoon sunshine', the most reliable forecast in California. Locals name the months: May Gray, June Gloom. The layer is a natural air conditioner for coastal cities and a water source for coastal redwoods, which harvest its fog drip. Its depth is exquisitely sensitive to the strength of the high offshore, which is why a change of 100 metres in inversion height is the difference between a grey day at the beach and a sunny one.
Why do autumn cold fronts seem so much stronger than spring ones? September's front dropped us 25 degrees.

The fronts themselves aren't necessarily stronger — the contrast they separate is. Through summer, the air over a continent bakes to its annual maximum while the polar regions begin their long cooling. By early autumn, the temperature gradient between the still-summer air mass and the first genuinely arctic air masses is near its yearly peak, and the jet stream — which lives on that gradient — is spinning back up after its summer slackening.

So a September or October front can have tropical-feeling air at 30 °C on one side and air that was over the Canadian Arctic a few days earlier on the other, with a strengthening jet overhead to drive the system. In spring the geometry reverses: the continent is still cold, the returning warm air is comparatively feeble, and the gradient — while real — is usually less extreme than autumn's collision of summer's stored heat against winter's first advance. The drama also has a human component: a 25-degree drop from 32 °C feels like a season changing in a day, because it is.
Why is the beach cooler than inland on summer days but milder at night?

Water's thermal inertia runs the whole show. Sand and soil heat up and cool down quickly — a thin surface layer holds the day's heat. Water mixes: sunshine is absorbed through metres of ocean and stirred by waves and currents, so the sea surface temperature changes only slowly through the season, and barely at all between day and night.

By day, the land out-heats the sea, the hot air over land rises, and the sea breeze imports the ocean's coolth to the beach — the shoreline sits near the water's temperature while inland towns run 5–10 °C hotter. At night the land radiates its shallow heat away quickly, but the sea surface is essentially the same temperature it was at noon, so coastal air stays mild, sometimes warmer than the inland valleys where cold air has pooled. The coast lives next to a thermostat set to the season's average; inland lives next to a stovetop. It's also why coastal climates have small daily and annual ranges, and why a sea breeze arriving is the most dependable appointment in summer weather.
El Niño is forecast for this winter. What can that actually tell me about MY winter, and what can't it?

El Niño — anomalously warm water across the equatorial Pacific — reorganises the tropical convection that drives the jet streams, and those teleconnections tilt regional odds for a season. The classic North American pattern: a stronger, more southerly jet across the southern U.S. (wetter, stormier winters for California and the Gulf Coast), a weaker polar jet intrusion into the northern tier (milder winters for the northern U.S. and Canada), and suppressed Atlantic hurricane activity via increased shear. La Niña roughly reverses the tilts.

Now the honest limits. These are probability shifts over a whole season, not schedules: an El Niño winter in the north still contains arctic outbreaks, and a 'wet' California signal is an average over storms that arrive or don't. The strength of the event matters (weak events tilt weakly), other patterns (the Arctic Oscillation, the Madden-Julian Oscillation) can override it for weeks at a time, and the signal is stronger in some regions than others — the Pacific Northwest's El Niño dryness is less reliable than the southern tier's wetness. Used correctly, it's a planning tilt for reservoirs, energy, and agriculture. Used as 'El Niño means my town floods in February', it's astrology with better physics.
Can I really use cloud types as a map of the atmosphere? What do the main families tell me?

Yes — clouds are the visible part of the atmosphere's vertical structure, and the genera sort by altitude into three families. High clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), above roughly 6 km, are made of ice crystals: thin, wispy, fibrous, often the first sign of an approaching warm front or the debris of distant storms. Middle clouds (altocumulus, altostratus), roughly 2–6 km, are water or mixed: altostratus is the grey sheet that makes the sun look like it's behind frosted glass, classically thickening ahead of rain. Low clouds (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus) live below 2 km: stratus is a fog-like layer, nimbostratus is the deep grey rain-maker.

Then the vertical family breaks the level scheme: cumulus and cumulonimbus grow upward through the levels on convection, and their height is their message — shallow cumulus humilis means a stable, fair day; towering cumulonimbus means the whole column is unstable. Read together, the sky tells you what's happening at several heights at once. A morning sequence of cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus is literally a cross-section of a warm front approaching, drawn in cloud.
I can see streaks of rain under the clouds but the ground stays dry. What's happening up there?

That's virga — precipitation falling from cloud that evaporates (or, for ice, sublimates) before reaching the ground. The streaks curve because the falling particles enter layers of different wind and because evaporation shrinks them and slows their fall.

Virga is common where the air beneath the cloud is dry — high deserts are famous for it — and it's not just a curiosity. Evaporation chills the air it passes through, and that cooled air can descend in downdrafts; virga showers are a classic source of dry microbursts, where the first sign of a storm's punch at the surface is wind, not rain. Virga also marks a moistening process: each shower humidifies the layer a little, so after hours of virga the air may finally be moist enough for rain to survive the trip — forecasters watch virga on radar as the atmosphere 'priming' itself. The dark, jellyfish-tendril look under a cloud deck is the atmosphere raining into its own dry air and losing.
I saw mammatus clouds after a storm and someone said it means a tornado is coming. True?

Mostly myth. Mammatus are the pouch-like lobes hanging from the underside of a cloud — most dramatically under a thunderstorm's anvil. They form where pockets of cloud air, cooled by evaporation and laden with ice crystals, sink gently into drier air below: each pouch is a small, slow downdraft, the cloud's underside sagging in lobes. They're often most spectacular after the storm's worst has passed, lit by a low sun.

The tornado association is a misunderstanding of proximity: mammatus appear on severe thunderstorms because severe storms have big, icy anvils, not because the pouches spawn tornadoes. The storms that produce mammatus can also produce tornadoes — but from their rotating updrafts, not from the anvil's underbelly, and mammatus also decorate harmless storms and even non-thunderstorm clouds. Treat them as a sign of turbulence and a turbulent sky worth admiring from safety, not as a warning signal. The real visual warnings are a rotating wall cloud and a persistent, organised lowering — different structures entirely.
There's a perfect ring around the sun today. Old-timers say it means rain is coming. Are they right?

Often enough that the lore survived. The ring is a 22° halo, formed by sunlight refracting through hexagonal ice crystals in cirrostratus cloud — a high, thin, uniform sheet of ice cloud. The crystals bend light by a minimum of about 22 degrees, which is why the ring has that fixed radius and a sharp inner edge.

The forecasting value isn't the halo itself but what cirrostratus announces: high moisture streaming in aloft, classically the leading edge of a warm front's cloud shield. In the classic sequence — cirrus thickening into cirrostratus (halo visible), lowering into altostratus (halo gone, sun a dim disc), then rain — the halo appears roughly 12–24 hours before the rain arrives. It isn't infallible: cirrostratus can come from other patterns, including jet-stream moisture that never organises into a front. But 'ring around the sun or moon, rain before long' is one of the folk rules with a real physical chain behind it. A ring around the moon works identically and is easier to look at.
Some jet contrails vanish in seconds and others spread into cloud that lasts for hours. What are the long ones telling me?

A contrail is an exhaust-mixed cloud: jet exhaust adds water vapour and particles to very cold air, and if the mixture saturates, a line of ice cloud forms. What happens next reads out the humidity of the air at cruising altitude, roughly 9–12 km up.

If the ambient air is dry, the contrail's ice crystals sublimate quickly into it — the trail fades in seconds to minutes. If the air at that level is already near saturation, the crystals can't evaporate; the trail persists, spreads in the wind shear, and can widen into a sheet of cirrus lasting hours. So persistent, spreading contrails are a free upper-air observation: the high atmosphere is moist, which in many patterns is an early sign of an approaching system — the same moisture that produces natural cirrus ahead of a warm front. Contrails also genuinely matter for climate accounting, since the persistent ones form cirrus that traps outgoing radiation. Next time you see the sky cross-hatched with old trails, you're looking at a humidity measurement written across the whole sky.
There are smooth, lens-shaped clouds parked over the mountain ridge that never move, even in strong wind. How can a cloud stand still in a gale?

It doesn't — the air moves through it. Those are lenticular clouds, formed in mountain waves. When stable air is forced over a ridge, it oscillates on the lee side like water flowing over a submerged rock: up, down, up, down, in a train of standing waves. At each wave crest, the rising air cools to saturation and a cloud forms; descending past the crest, it warms and the cloud evaporates. The cloud is a standing pattern, continuously manufactured at its upwind edge and dissolved at its downwind edge — a fountain shape, not an object.

The stacked 'pile of plates' versions form when several moist layers ride the same wave. For pilots, lenticulars are a warning sign: they mark powerful wave motion and severe turbulence, especially in the rotor clouds that can form beneath the wave crests. For observers they're a free diagram of invisible airflow — and they can appear far downwind of the range that made them, hovering over flat country like the famous UFO reports they inspire.
'Red sky at night, sailor's delight; red sky in the morning, sailors take warning.' Is there real physics in that?

There is, with a latitude attached. The redness itself is optics: at sunrise and sunset, sunlight crosses a long path through the atmosphere, and scattering removes the blue, leaving reds and oranges to light the clouds — but only if the air in the direction of the sun is clear and dry enough to let that light through.

The forecast logic rides on mid-latitude weather moving west to east. At sunset (red sky at night), the sun is in the west — the direction your weather comes from. Red light reaching you means the western air is clear and dry: high pressure and fair weather are upstream and approaching. At sunrise, the red light comes from the east — clear air behind you, departing — while the clouds being lit are often the shield of a system approaching from the west. So the rhyme encodes 'fair weather coming' versus 'fair weather leaving'.

Its limits: it assumes the prevailing westerlies (tropics, where weather moves east to west, flip it), it says nothing about timing beyond a day or so, and local effects can fake it. Within its home territory, though, it's a legitimate piece of compressed meteorology — which is presumably why versions of it are thousands of years old.
Some cumulus clouds stay small and flat all day while others explode upward. How do I tell which kind I'm looking at by noon?

Watch the tops and the proportions. Fair-weather cumulus (cumulus humilis) are wider than they are tall, with flat bases and gently domed, well-defined tops — they look like floating cotton tufts and they stay that way because a stable layer or warm cap above them flattens their growth; the atmosphere is letting thermals rise a little and no further.

Building cumulus (cumulus congestus) are taller than wide, with hard, cauliflower tops that keep boiling upward and sharp outlines — the cap is weak or absent and parcels are accelerating. Details that matter by noon: if the towers are leaning hard, shear is strong; if the edges look fuzzy and evaporate as fast as they grow, the air aloft is dry and the storms may starve; if bases darken and merge and the towers keep hardening hour by hour, expect showers or storms by afternoon. The single best noon question is 'are they taller than they were an hour ago, and taller than they are wide?' Growth plus vertical dominance is the atmosphere telling you the lid is coming off.
What's the difference between a shelf cloud and a wall cloud? They both look like the storm is lowering toward the ground.

The distinction is safety-critical, and it's about rotation and attachment. A shelf cloud is the leading edge of the storm's outflow — a long, wedge-shaped band attached to the front of the rain area, formed where the gust front's cold air lifts warm air. It marks strong outflow winds arriving, often with a sudden temperature drop and gust — but the shelf itself is not rotating and is not a tornado precursor. It typically stretches along the whole storm front and moves with the gust front.

A wall cloud hangs beneath the storm's updraft, usually toward the rear flank of a supercell, separated from the rain. It's a local lowering — often a kilometre or two across — and the key observation is slow, persistent rotation. A rotating wall cloud is the mesocyclone reaching down; tornadoes form from these. Field test: shelf clouds advance along a line and bring wind; wall clouds sit in one part of the storm and turn. If you see a lowering and can't tell, watch for rotation for 30 seconds — and regardless, a storm close enough to inspect is a storm to be inside shelter for.
The sky turned green during a severe storm. I've heard that means a tornado for sure. Does it?

The green is real; the certainty is folklore. Severe storms sometimes take on a green or aqua cast, and while the phenomenon is well documented photographically, the exact optics are still debated — the leading explanation combines the storm's deep column of water and hail (which absorbs and scatters light selectively, favouring blue-green) with the warm, yellow-red light of a low sun behind or beside the storm. Blue storm-light plus yellow sunlight can sum to green.

What the colour does reliably indicate is a tall, water-loaded storm — the kind with heavy rain and often large hail, since a deep column of hydrometeors is needed to tint the light. Hail is the strongest association in the observational record. Tornadoes, however, occur in plenty of non-green storms, and most green storms never produce one. So treat green light as a marker of a genuinely severe storm overhead — a reason to be in shelter — not as a tornado detector. The warnings that matter remain radar-indicated or observed rotation, and official warnings. Colour is the atmosphere's mood lighting, not its instrument panel.
We just had the coldest week in a decade. Doesn't that argue against global warming?

No — because weather and climate answer different questions. Weather is the state of the atmosphere this week; climate is the statistics of weather over decades. A warming climate shifts the whole distribution of temperatures, but the distribution still has a cold tail, and circulation patterns can still park arctic air over your region for a week. A single cold snap is one draw from the distribution; it carries almost no information about how the distribution is moving.

Two clarifications help. First, the relevant comparison is rates: in recent decades, daily record highs in the U.S. have outnumbered record lows by roughly two to one, which is what a shifting distribution looks like from inside it — cold records still occur, just less often than they used to, while warm records pile up. Second, some researchers have debated whether a warming Arctic could occasionally favour the wavy jet patterns that deliver cold outbreaks — that hypothesis is contested, but even its proponents are describing weather patterns operating within a warming baseline. Judge the climate claim by the 30-year trend lines, not by this week's very real, very cold weather.
When a study says climate change 'made this heatwave five times more likely', what did the scientists actually do?

They ran a counterfactual. Attribution studies take the observed event — say, a heatwave of a given intensity over a given region — and model two worlds: the real one, with current greenhouse gas concentrations, and a counterfactual one without human-caused warming. In each world they run many simulations and count how often an event this extreme occurs. If it happens in 1% of simulated years in the counterfactual world and 5% in ours, the event was made five times more likely; the 'fraction of attributable risk' is the share of the current probability that wouldn't exist without warming (here, 80%).

Note what the claim is and isn't. It is not 'climate change caused this heatwave' — heatwaves happen in both worlds, driven by weather patterns. It's a statement about loaded dice: the background warming raised the baseline temperature, so a circulation pattern that once produced a hot week now produces a record one, more often. The method is strongest for heat (a direct thermodynamic signal), decent for extreme rainfall, and weakest for phenomena like tornadoes where the physics is small-scale and the records are short. Read the number as a probability shift, and it says exactly what it means.
My weather app shows 'normal high: 84' for today. Normal according to whom, and why did it change from a few years ago?

Those are climate normals: 30-year averages of temperature, precipitation, and other variables, computed by national weather services for thousands of stations. The standard is set by the World Meteorological Organization, and the current U.S. normals cover 1991–2020. They're recalculated every decade, so the set you saw a few years ago was 1981–2010 — and yes, for most U.S. locations the newer normals are warmer, because the 2010s were warmer than the 1980s were.

That moving window is deliberate: normals are meant to describe the climate a farmer, engineer, or forecaster should plan around now, not a fixed historical baseline. The side effect is worth noticing: by chasing the warming, each new set of normals makes current anomalies look smaller — a month that's 2 degrees above the 1991–2020 normal would have been further above the 1951–1980 one. Scientists tracking long-term change therefore usually compare against older fixed baselines, while your app's 'normal' answers the practical question: what should you expect on this date in the climate we currently live in?
Can you give me a clean way to explain weather versus climate to my kid?

Try this: weather is what you wear today; climate is what's in your closet. Weather is the atmosphere's state over hours to days — this afternoon's thunderstorm, Saturday's cold front. Climate is the long-term pattern those days add up to over at least 30 years — how often fronts come, how hot Julys run, whether winters bring snow or rain.

A few analogies that hold up: weather is your mood today; climate is your personality. Weather is one hand of cards; climate is the deck you're drawing from. And the one that handles the common confusion: a single cold day in a warming climate is like losing one hand with a stacked deck — it happens, and it tells you almost nothing about the deck. The definition that scientists actually use is close to the closet version: climate is the statistics of weather — the averages, the extremes, and how often each occurs — over decades. Change the deck slowly and the hands change with it, one unremarkable day at a time.
If the climate is warming, how can we still get enormous snowstorms? Shouldn't snow be disappearing?

Snow needs two things — cold air and moisture — and warming attacks one while feeding the other. Warmer air holds more water vapour: the saturation capacity rises about 7% per °C (the Clausius-Clapeyron relation). As long as a storm's air is still below freezing, a warmer, moister atmosphere can deliver more snow, not less — the biggest snowstorms historically occur with temperatures just below freezing, not in deep arctic air, because very cold air is too dry to snow hard.

So the observed pattern makes sense: the snow season shrinks at the edges (later first snow, earlier melt, more winter rain at the margins), average totals decline in many mid-latitude regions, yet individual blockbuster storms remain possible and can even be juiced by extra moisture — including storms drawing on warmer ocean water. What warming reliably removes is the frequency of cold-enough air, which is why the long-term trend and the single huge storm are not in conflict. The storm is weather; the shrinking season is climate; both observations fit in the same physics.
Why do scientists point to the ratio of record highs to record lows as a climate fingerprint? Records get broken in a stable climate too.

They do — and that's exactly the baseline the fingerprint is measured against. In a stable climate, record-breaking doesn't stop: with long station records, new daily records still occur by chance, but highs and lows should occur at roughly equal rates over time, each getting rarer as records lengthen. It's a fair coin that slowly lands less often.

In the observed U.S. record, the coin isn't fair anymore. Analyses of daily records across thousands of stations found that by the 2000s, record highs were occurring about twice as often as record lows — and the imbalance grows decade by decade. In a warming world that's the expected signature: the whole temperature distribution shifts warm, so its hot tail crosses old thresholds often while its cold tail reaches old records rarely. The test is powerful because it's simple counting, insensitive to thermometer changes that complicate average-temperature records. A stable climate predicts 1:1 over the long run; a cooling climate would predict the reverse. The measured ratio is one of those statistics that's hard to explain any other way.
Global temperature is up over a degree, but my town's records don't show anything like that. Who's right?

Both can be — you're comparing different quantities. The global figure is an average over the whole planet, and warming is geographically uneven: the Arctic has warmed several times faster than the global rate, land warms faster than ocean, and some regions — parts of the southeastern U.S. are a studied example, sometimes called a 'warming hole' — have warmed little over the twentieth century, plausibly due to a mix of aerosols, land use, and natural variability.

Your town's record also carries extra noise: a single station's 30-year trend has wide error bars from year-to-year variability alone, plus possible non-climate jumps if the station moved or the town grew around it (the urban heat island adds its own local trend, usually upward). The right comparison is your region's multi-station average over many decades against the global one. Local trend differing from the global mean is expected — the global mean is nobody's local weather. But the reverse inference doesn't work either: one town's flat record doesn't dent a planetary average built from thousands of stations, ships, buoys, and satellites.
Our lilacs bloom two weeks earlier than my grandmother remembers. Is that climate data or just nostalgia?

It's potentially real data — phenology, the timing of biological seasons, is one of the more sensitive climate indicators, because plants integrate temperature over weeks rather than reacting to a single day. Lilacs are actually a formal instrument: networks of cloned lilacs (genetically identical plants) have been planted across North America precisely so that bloom-date differences reflect climate, not genetics. Long records of lilac and honeysuckle first bloom, grape harvest dates in Europe, and cherry blossom dates in Kyoto — the last kept for over a thousand years — consistently show spring events advancing in recent decades, on the order of days per decade in many regions.

The caveats are the honest ones: a garden's microclimate changes as trees and buildings grow around it, memory compresses, and one plant in one yard is an anecdote. But when her observation lines up with the cloned-lilac network, the orchard records, and the temperature trend all pointing the same way, the anecdote is corroborated. Grandmothers, it turns out, keep decent phenological records.
